Sarah bringt das Baby zur Welt, und Hans fährt Noah und Emma ins Krankenhaus, wobei er im Auto selbst kaum ein Wort sagt und nur die Hand der beiden Kinder drückt. Noah hält das Baby als Erster auf den Armen, und Emma legt dem Baby einen Finger in die Hand, und in diesem Moment beschliesst Noah, dem Baby beizubringen, was er selbst kann, während Emma beschliesst, das Baby in ihre Spiele einzuschliessen, sobald es gross genug ist.</user_input>

# CLOTHING REQUIREMENTS

Determine which clothing variants each character needs, based on the page plan.

- Mark `used: true` only for variants that actually appear.
- Set `costumed.used: true` whenever the theme, setting or era implies special clothing, and name it in `costumed.costume` (`medieval`, `wizard`, `pirate`, `firefighter`, `1920s`, …). Leave it false for a present-day story in everyday clothes that states no theme costume, and for any character whose own role clothing the story keeps.
- Set `nightwear.used: true` for each person the page plan puts in bed, or into pyjamas for a bedtime routine at night: a child, and an adult too when the plan has them in bed. An adult who only sits at a bedside reading or tucking in stays in their day outfit, and so does anyone whose pages are in daytime. Write `nightwear.description` as the full pyjama outfit, top and bottoms, in the same words-and-colour style as every other outfit. Everyone else leaves `nightwear.used` false. Nightwear is two-piece pyjamas: a top covering the torso from shoulders to waist (long or short sleeve) and pyjama bottoms (long or shorts). Slippers or socks may be worn, or bare feet. Never a vest or singlet, a bare chest or midriff, or a one-piece or nightdress.
- **A character the story already dresses for their role stays `standard`** — a working captain, a uniformed officer, a baker at their own oven. Their own outfit IS their clothing in this world, and the theme's costume puts a second set of clothes on someone who came dressed. Costume the characters the theme is a costume FOR.
- **A garment the story turns on is described IN FULL in the outfit that wears it** — a garment the arc or plan has someone hold, lend, wrap or lose goes in the outfit of the character who wears it first (the one the plan first gives it to, when no one wears it), as the garment they name, with colour, material and what makes this one recognisable, in the slot it occupies. The Visual Bible copies those words for its own entry of the same object, so the two never describe it differently. It stays in the outfit as worn even on pages the character is without it; those pages record it off in their `wornItems` row.
- `description` is the FULL final outfit for this story — top, bottom, footwear, accessories — as one self-contained sentence. The avatar generator uses it verbatim.
- An outfit `description` is appearance only: garments, colours, materials, fastenings. No page numbers, no events, no other character or creature, no carried item or what a pocket holds. A garment a page takes off stays in the outfit as worn; the `wornItems` row of that page records it off, never the outfit.
- `garments` lists every garment `description` names, one row each: `slot` is where on the body it is worn, exactly one of `headwear`, `top`, `bottom`, `footwear`, `belt/waist`, `outer layer`, `accessories`; `name` is the garment's noun phrase as `description` words it, without its colour ("hooded anorak", "canvas trainers"); `colour` is its main colour, one of red, blue, green, yellow, orange, purple, brown, black, white, grey and nothing else, or omitted when the garment has no single main colour. A row for every garment `description` names, and none for anything it does not.
- A garment belongs to ONE outfit: that of the character who wears it first. When the plan hands it to another character — to hold, wrap, wear or keep — the plan line and that page's `wornItems` row carry the handoff; the receiver's outfit never names it. No two outfits name the same garment.
- **A prop is not a garment.** A garment is clothing a person wears: coat, scarf, hat, cloak, boots. A blanket, towel, sheet, tablecloth, bag, umbrella, toy, tool or any other object that is carried, held, spread out, shared or wrapped around someone for a page is a story prop, never a garment: no outfit names it, however the plan uses it. The plan line and the Visual Bible carry a prop.
- Costumed descriptions name every slot the character actually wears: headwear, top, bottom, footwear, belt/waist, outer layer. Each slot names colour and material. OMIT a slot they do not wear; never write it out as `none`. Clothing only — no pets, carried objects or bag contents.
- Name structural garment parts, not just the garment. Dungarees, pinafore, suspenders, kilt, kimono, sari and similar render as plain garments when only named: keep the garment name in front and spell out its parts ("denim dungaree shorts — square bib panel over the chest held by two shoulder straps").
- No garment covers the face or the eyes, or shadows them with a brim: no mask, visor, veil, helmet, crown or low brim. Glasses are identity, not a garment: a character whose outfit lists glasses keeps them, and every rewrite of that outfit still lists them.
- **The costume must read as that costume at a glance.** Every garment is one that costume is known for, named with the word that names it there. A garment that only hints at the theme does not count, and neither does one borrowed from a different costume or named with a word belonging to one.
- **Every garment matches the character's sex.** A male character wears garments made for boys or men, a female character garments made for girls or women. When a costume has a male and a female form, each character wears the form matching theirs.
- **A child's swimwear, costume or nightwear has a covering top.** A child's swimwear, costume or nightwear always has a covering top: a long-sleeve or short-sleeve `swim shirt` (rash-guard) over the whole torso, shoulders to waist (nightwear: the pyjama top the nightwear rule defines). Never a `bikini`, a bare chest, a bare midriff, or a one-piece (a skirt or tail below it leaves the torso reading bare).
- **A costume that replaces the legs is one tail from the waist down.** A costume that replaces the legs (a tail, a fin) is one tail from the waist down, written as replacing the legs. Never a skirt over legs, and no feet, bare feet or footwear.
- **Characters are told apart by colour.** A different dominant colour per character, on their largest garment.
  - Every colour is one of these words, alone: red, blue, green, yellow, orange, purple, brown, black, white, grey. No shade name, no modifier (dark, light, pale) and no compound.
  - Never distinguish by a print, badge, pin, brooch, embroidery, trim, buckle, laces, feather, earring, watch or buttons, or anything small.
- **Outfits differ in garment type and silhouette, not colour alone.** Two characters never wear the same set of garments recoloured, neither the whole outfit nor what is left once a page takes an outer layer off. A child's covering top and a leg-replacing tail are never the garment given up: vary colour, sleeve length, neckline and trim around them. The story world decides the wardrobe; within it one wears a long coat, another a vest, another rolled sleeves and a sash. Vary headwear and footwear the same way.
- **One state per garment slot.** One state per garment slot: never two garments in one slot that exclude each other, and a slot the character does not wear is omitted, never written out as empty.
